title: The operating system as traffic warden
story:
Several programs want the same processor, the same memory and the same devices, and none of them can be trusted to take only its share or to stay within its own memory. One program owns the hardware and hands out access to the rest. That is the whole job, and the three things it hands out are time on the processor, a private view of memory, and a uniform way to reach devices.

Ritchie and Thompson described the system that fixed the shape of all this in Communications of the ACM in 1974, listing among its distinguishing features a hierarchical file system incorporating demountable volumes; compatible file, device and inter-process input and output; the ability to initiate asynchronous processes; a system command language selectable on a per-user basis; and over one hundred subsystems including a dozen languages. Read that list as a set of decisions rather than a description, because each one is still with you.

A correction while we are here, since the phrase is repeated constantly. The slogan that everything is a file does not appear in that paper. What appears is compatible file, device and inter-process input and output — which is what the slogan compresses, and the longer form is more useful because it says what the compatibility is between. The paper also has a version problem worth knowing about: it was a revised version of one presented at the Fourth Symposium on Operating Systems Principles in 1973, and was revised again for a later journal printing, so the copy most often circulated is not the 1974 text and describes different hardware.

The mechanism that makes the arrangement enforceable rather than merely conventional is a boundary. The hardware runs in two modes, and the instructions that touch devices, change memory mappings or alter the scheduler are available in only one of them. A program asks for those things by making a call that crosses the boundary, which is the moment the system gets to check. Without that hardware distinction, an operating system would be advice rather than a warden — any program could simply take what it wanted.

What that costs is a crossing on every interaction with the outside world. Reading a byte from a device is not a function call, it is a transition into another mode, a check, work on your behalf, and a transition back. This is why batching matters everywhere in this track, and why the storage lesson and the networking lessons keep arriving at the same advice: the fixed cost is per crossing, so ask fewer times for more.

problem.name: Resource arbitration
problem.shape: Multiple programs need exclusive use of shared hardware, and none can be trusted to limit itself.
tell: two programs must not see each other's memory
a device has one consumer at a time and many would-be users
a program must be stoppable without its cooperation
a call to read or write is being made in a tight loop
problem.move: Let one privileged program own the hardware and mediate every access, so that scheduling, memory mapping and device access are all requested rather than taken. Then batch requests, because each one crosses a protection boundary whose cost is fixed and independent of how much you ask for.
problem.invariant: The privileged instructions are unavailable in the mode ordinary programs run in, so mediation is enforced by hardware rather than by agreement. Without that distinction the system is advice.
problem.breaks: The boundary protects programs from each other and does not protect them from the system's own abstractions. A uniform interface over files, devices and pipes means the same call can cost a microsecond or a hundred milliseconds, and the interface gives no indication which — so correctness is guaranteed where performance is not even hinted at.

cost.time: a mode transition and a check on every interaction with the outside world, which is why batching is the recurring advice in this track
cost.space: per-process bookkeeping — memory maps, open file tables, scheduling state
cost.beats: cooperative sharing, which works until one program misbehaves, and giving each program its own machine, which is what containers later approximate at much lower cost

worked.problem: What is the operating system actually protecting, and from whom?
worked.reasoning:
Three things, from three different threats, and it is worth separating them because they are usually collapsed into a vague notion of safety.

Memory, from other programs. Each process gets its own view of the address space, so one program cannot read or corrupt another's data — including the system's own. This is the protection people usually mean, and it is the one that makes a multi-user machine possible at all.

The processor, from any single program. Without intervention a program that never yields simply keeps the processor. The system takes it back by force, on a timer, which is what makes the machine responsive regardless of how badly any individual program behaves. Note the direction: this protects every other program from one program's selfishness, and the selfishness need not be malicious — an infinite loop is enough.

Devices, from concurrent and incorrect use. Two programs writing to the same disk region, or issuing conflicting commands to the same controller, produce corruption rather than contention. The system serialises access and presents a uniform interface so that no program has to know the device's command protocol.

The mechanism underneath all three is the hardware's mode distinction. Privileged instructions — touching devices, changing memory mappings, altering the scheduler — are unavailable in the mode ordinary programs run in. That is what converts the arrangement from convention into enforcement, and it is why the answer to whom is partly the programs themselves: the protection works against a program that is actively trying to violate it, not merely one that forgets.

What it does not protect is worth stating too, because it bounds the guarantee. It does not protect a program from itself — corrupting your own memory is permitted. It does not protect against a program consuming its fair share badly. And it does not protect against the uniform abstraction hiding costs, which is the practical failure engineers actually meet: the same read call may cost a microsecond from a cache or a hundred milliseconds from a remote device, and the interface is identical either way.

problem.practice: Time a loop that reads one byte at a time from a file a million times, then the same million bytes read in large blocks. The difference is almost entirely boundary crossings. Then look at how many distinct system calls your program actually makes during a typical request.

beats.broke: Many programs want the same processor, memory and devices at once, and none can be trusted to take only its share or stay inside its own memory.
beats.fix: Interpose one program that owns the hardware and hands out access — scheduling the processor, mapping memory per process, and presenting devices through a single uniform interface.
beats.cost: Every interaction with the hardware crosses a boundary that must be checked, so protection is paid for on every call, and the uniform interface hides differences that sometimes matter enormously.

interview.q: What is the operating system actually protecting, and from whom?
interview.trap: Answering only memory isolation. Three separate protections are running — memory from other programs, the processor from any one program, and devices from concurrent use — and the processor one is enforced by preemption precisely because a program need not be malicious to hold it forever.
interview.answer:
Three things, from three threats, and they are worth separating because they get collapsed into a vague notion of safety.

Memory, from other programs: each process gets its own view of the address space, so one cannot read or corrupt another's data, including the system's. That is the protection people usually mean and the one that makes a multi-user machine possible.

The mechanism under all three is the hardware's mode distinction. Privileged instructions — touching devices, changing memory mappings, altering the scheduler — are unavailable in the mode ordinary programs run in, which converts the arrangement from convention into enforcement. takeaway: One privileged program owns the hardware and everything else asks, which is enforceable only because the machine has a mode where the dangerous instructions do not exist — and the crossing is charged per request, not per byte.
